segments.title: The Fog and the Labyrinth: Bleak House's Opening World

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Charles Dickens' extraordinary 1853 novel — chapter by chapter, image by image, character by character.
Bleak House is a novel that rewards slowness — that asks you to sit with its fog, its darkness, its labyrinthine legal machinery.
And we have three remarkable guides to help us do exactly that.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing professor who is obsessed — in the best possible way — with how Dickens builds his effects.
She sees the architecture behind every sentence, and she will make you see it too.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who specialises in Victorian institutions — Chancery, the Poor Law, the whole machinery of nineteenth-century governance.
He brings the real world into the room, and occasionally a quiet, well-placed fury.
And Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime reading Dickens on Dickens' own terms — as a moral artist, not a pamphleteer.
He is, as you will discover, an exceedingly courteous man with exceedingly sharp opinions.
Today we begin at the beginning — with one of the most famous openings in all of fiction.
The fog of Bleak House: what it is, what it does, and why Dickens needed it.
What strikes me every time I return to that opening chapter is how ruthlessly Dickens refuses to give us a stable viewpoint.
Before we meet a single character, we are handed this extraordinary prose-poem of fog and mud and geological time.
He opens with the sentence — and I have it practically memorised at this point — in the setup for what follows:
"London. Michaelmas Term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall. Implacable November weather."
Those are noun phrases — not sentences — and that is a deliberate structural choice.
The grammar itself is fractured, incomplete — mirroring the world the novel is about to describe.
Nothing resolves into a proper subject and verb — just as nothing in Chancery ever resolves.
Eleanor is quite right about the legal mirror — but I want to add a historical dimension to that fog, because it is not merely atmospheric.
The fog Dickens describes — descending on the Essex Marshes, creeping up the Thames, settling over Lincoln's Inn — is a physical reality of mid-Victorian London.
The coal smoke, the river effluent, the sheer density of bodies in a city swelling beyond any previous human habitation — all of it produced a literally unbreathable atmosphere.
Dickens knew this.
And when he writes — and I think this is the passage that stops every reader cold —
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That word "defiled" — it is doing enormous moral work inside what looks like a landscape description.
The fog is not neutral weather — it has already been contaminated by the city it moves through.
I find myself in the unusual position of agreeing with both my colleagues, while wishing to resist a certain conclusion they may be drawing.
The fog is magnificent — yes.
But I am always slightly wary when the fog becomes a thesis, a symbol pointing in one predetermined political direction.
What Dickens gives us in that opening chapter is something stranger and more frightening than an indictment of institutions.
He gives us a vision of a world in which human beings cannot see one another.
Consider this passage — which I have always read as the true moral centre of the opening:
"And hard by Temple Bar, in Lincoln's Inn Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery."
The Lord Chancellor sits at the very heart of the fog — not outside it, not above it, but within it.
That is not a political argument — that is a moral and almost theological statement about the blindness of power.
Edmund, I think that is exactly right — and it brings me to the dual narration, which is the structural masterstroke Dickens deploys.
The third-person narrator of the opening chapters is omniscient, satirical, cosmically furious — a kind of Old Testament voice describing a fallen world.
Then Dickens switches — and we get Esther Summerson, writing in the first person, years after the events, with a warmth and a personal humility that is almost shocking by contrast.
Esther begins her own narrative with characteristic diffidence — she says:
"I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages, for I know I am not clever."
The irony, of course, is that she is writing the more penetrating half of the novel.
Her self-deprecation is itself a kind of structural irony that Dickens sustains for eight hundred pages.
That switch in narrative voice also maps, I think, onto a social distinction that is crucial to the novel's architecture.
The omniscient narrator describes the fog from above — a god's-eye view of the city as system.
Esther experiences it from the inside — she is a person to whom things happen, not an observer who comprehends the whole.
And that distinction — between systemic view and individual experience — is precisely the tension Dickens is dramatising when he introduces the case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
He describes it with magnificent savagery — the case has been going on so long that no one alive can remember its origin:
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means."
A scarecrow of a suit — that is not metaphor employed for decorative effect.
That is the carcass of something that was once alive, now preserved only to frighten off anyone who might come too close.
James's reading of Jarndyce and Jarndyce is acute — though I would add that the case is also something Dickens depicts as spiritually corrosive, not merely bureaucratically absurd.
What the suit does to Richard Carstone — that promising, warm-natured young man — is the novel's most devastating demonstration of character destroyed not by villainy but by hope.
Hope misdirected is Dickens' great subject in this novel, and it is introduced in the very first chapters.
There is a line about the litigants in Chancery that I find almost unbearable in its precision:
"Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here!"
That is Dickens speaking directly — breaking the satirical frame entirely — and the ferocity of it is all the more powerful for the restraint that surrounds it.
The fog disorients; the court destroys.
And what I find so thrilling about that moment is how it connects to the very grammar of the opening pages.
Dickens opens the novel without subject or verb — incomplete syntax — and then, when he finally addresses us directly, it is as a warning.
The whole formal architecture of the opening is building toward that imperative: suffer any wrong, but do not come here.
It is a novel that begins by announcing its own moral stakes before we have met its people.
And what a world those stakes create — fog, mud, legal labyrinth, and already the shadow of individual lives being consumed within it.

In our next segment, we'll follow the people who enter that world — the wards in Chancery, Esther, Ada, and Richard — and ask what Dickens does with innocence when he places it inside a machine designed to grind it down.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Chancery's Grip: How Law Destroys Character

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great Victorian panorama apart piece by piece.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into the novel's dark engine: the Court of Chancery and what it does to the people caught inside it.
With me are three extraordinary readers of this novel, and I want to introduce them properly.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — she wants to know exactly how every gear fits.

Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian of the Victorian era, and when we talk about Chancery, he can tell us not just what Dickens wrote but what was actually happening in that court — and it is not pretty.
And Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has lived with this novel for decades and remains convinced that its true subject is moral character under pressure, not institutional critique.
Edmund, I suspect that last point may be tested today.
Let's begin with the fog.
The fog in the opening chapter is one of the great architectural decisions in English fiction.
Dickens doesn't begin with a character or a plot — he begins with a condition.
Everything is fog before we meet a single person.
And then he gives us the sentence that does everything at once.
"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition of this High Court of Chancery."
He has fused the physical atmosphere of London with the moral atmosphere of the court in a single stroke.
And what's thrilling is that the fog never becomes purely metaphorical — it stays literal and symbolic simultaneously throughout the whole novel.
What makes that passage so effective is that it was, historically, not much of an exaggeration.
The Court of Chancery by the 1850s had cases pending that had been filed in the previous century.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce in the novel is hyperbole only at the margins.
There were real estates where the legal costs consumed the entire inheritance before a verdict was ever reached.
Dickens captures that institutional indifference with clinical precision when he writes of the court's suitors.
"Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here."
That is not a satirist's flourish — it is a practical warning from someone who had done his research.
I don't dispute the historical accuracy — James knows that territory far better than I do.
But I want to resist the reading in which Chancery is the novel's villain and all the characters are simply its victims.
Because if that were Dickens' real argument, Richard Carstone would be a tragedy of circumstance.
And Richard is not that.
Richard is a young man with a genuinely weak will who chooses, again and again, to make the suit his substitute for effort.
Jarndyce sees it absolutely clearly and says as much — that the suit has become Richard's excuse not to become anything.
"It is the character of such a suit to involve the suitor in a feeling of distrust, suspicion, and — I will add — contempt of himself."
Chancery does not destroy Richard — it provides the conditions in which Richard's own character destroys him.
Edmund, I find that reading morally bracing, but I think it lets the institution off rather lightly.
Because Dickens is careful to show us a spectrum of characters exposed to Chancery, and they don't all have Richard's particular weakness.
Miss Flite is arguably saner than the court that has imprisoned her in hope.
Gridley — the Man from Shropshire — is a man of enormous force of character and Chancery grinds him into the ground regardless.
What I love about Gridley's confrontation in court is the structural irony Dickens builds into it.
"I have been dragged for five and twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the use of my limbs from the torture."
The court's response is not cruelty — it's indifference, which Dickens presents as far worse.
An institution that doesn't notice its victims is more frightening than one that does.
Eleanor is absolutely right about Gridley, and his case illuminates something important about how Chancery functioned as a system.
The court could not be held responsible by any individual within it.
Each solicitor, each clerk, each Master in Chancery was only following procedure.
The diffusion of responsibility is precisely what made genuine reform so difficult for so long.
And Dickens understood that structural evasion perfectly — he gives it to Mr. Vholes, Richard's solicitor, with a horror that is almost satirical.
"The name of Vholes, his horse's name, and his father's name are so many tokens of the solidity of his professional character."
The respectability of a man who is, in every practical sense, a parasite feeding on Richard's delusion.
That is not Richard's weakness speaking — that is the machinery of an institution that profits from prolonging ruin.
I grant you Vholes — he is genuinely repellent, and Dickens renders him with a cold loathing that is quite different from his treatment of comic villains.
But I return always to Jarndyce himself as the novel's counter-argument.
Here is a man whose entire inheritance is consumed by the same suit, who has every reason for bitterness, and who has made himself into a figure of extraordinary practical goodness.
Dickens is telling us something vital about the relationship between will and circumstance.
He describes Jarndyce's settled policy in this way.
"It's in repose that I am Jarndyce of Bleak House, and there I find my own character."
That sense of moral repose as a deliberate achievement — built against the pressure of the court — is, for me, the novel's most important statement.
That is beautifully put, and I don't want to argue against Jarndyce's goodness.
But notice what it costs him — he retreats to Bleak House physically whenever the court's shadow falls.
His goodness is preserved by a kind of strategic withdrawal from the very system he cannot defeat.
That is not a solution — it is a coping mechanism.
The novel never provides a moment where good character confronts Chancery and actually wins.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce ends only when the estate is entirely consumed — when there is literally nothing left to litigate over.
That is not moral triumph — that is the court running out of fuel.
Eleanor has put her finger on something that I think needs underlining for modern listeners.
The resolution of the case by exhaustion of funds was not a narrative device — it was the actual mechanism by which many real Chancery suits concluded.
The court did not produce justice; it produced an eventual absence of contest.
And the human cost — the Jo-level cost — is what Dickens refuses to let us forget.
Jo has nothing to do with the suit, but he exists in the same infected atmosphere — the fog reaches him too.
Dickens writes of him in a passage of barely controlled fury.

"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
That rhetorical hammer — the anaphora of 'Dead' — is Dickens holding his whole society to account, not just the court.
That passage always stops me.
Whatever one's view of the novel's political programme, there is no honest reading of Jo's death that leaves one comfortable.
I would only add that the humanity of that passage comes from its particularity — it is this boy, this death, this moment.
Not a statistic, not a type — a person.
And that, I would argue, is where Dickens' genius lies — not in the systemic argument but in the irreducible individual.
I think that's the tension that makes Bleak House so permanently alive — it refuses to resolve neatly between those two readings.
The institution and the individual both matter, and both are implicated.

Coming up, we're going to look at the novel's other great structural device — the dual narration — and what it means that Dickens splits this story between an omniscient voice and Esther Summerson's intimate testimony.

segments.title: A Woman's Secrets: Lady Dedlock's Concealment and Unraveling

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens' great novel apart — and puts it back together again, richer for the looking.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most haunting figures: Lady Dedlock.
The grande dame of Chesney Wold, wrapped in boredom, draped in silk, concealing a secret that will ultimately destroy her.
Our three guests bring very different ways of reading her.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and critic who watches Dickens build his effects the way a master architect lays a foundation — she'll show us how Lady Dedlock is constructed on the page.
Professor James Blackstone brings the social and legal world that makes Lady Dedlock's predicament not merely melodrama but grim historical reality.
And Sir Edmund Leigh reads her as Dickens himself may have intended — a moral study of what concealment does to the soul.
Eleanor — Lady Dedlock is introduced to us almost as a type, a social category made flesh.
How does Dickens set her up — and then complicate her?
What Dickens does with Lady Dedlock in those opening chapters is extraordinarily controlled.
He introduces her through the third-person narrator — the omniscient, sardonic voice — and he gives her the great disease of her class: boredom.

The narrator tells us she has been at the centre of fashionable intelligence, that she has been presented at court, that Chesney Wold with all its grandeur has become — in that devastating phrase — quite another affair.
"My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in familiar conversation, our place in Lincolnshire."
That 'our place' — said with such proprietorial languor — tells you everything about the performance she's giving the world.
She owns it, she's bored by it, and she wears that boredom like armour.
But the genius is in what cracks that armour: a piece of handwriting on a legal document.
Something so small, so accidental, and her composure shatters before she can stop it.
Dickens makes the architecture of concealment visible in that single moment of involuntary recognition.
And we should be precise about what that handwriting represents — because the stakes are not merely emotional, they are entirely material.
Lady Dedlock's secret is that she had a child before her marriage — a child she believes to be dead, who is in fact Esther Summerson.
In the 1840s and 1850s, the social annihilation attached to that secret was not metaphorical.
A woman in her position, discovered to have had an illegitimate child, would have been expelled from every drawing room in England overnight.
Her husband could have separated from her, stripped her of social standing, and — crucially — denied her access to all the legal protections of her marriage.
Tulkinghorn, of course, understands this with perfect clarity.
He is Dickens' most chilling portrait of the law as pure instrument of power — not justice, not even profit, simply the pleasure of possession.
Dickens writes of him that he is of what is called the old school — a phrase
"a hard grained man, close, dry, and silent."
Those three adjectives are almost geological — you feel the weight of centuries of the legal profession in them.
James is right about the material stakes, but I would resist the temptation to make Lady Dedlock primarily a victim of social structure.
Dickens is too honest a moralist for that.
What Lady Dedlock suffers she suffers partly — only partly, I grant — through her own choices.
She chose concealment over confession, social elevation over honest poverty, a marriage of convenience over the acknowledgment of her daughter.
And those choices have a cumulative moral weight that Dickens does not flinch from.
There is that extraordinary passage when Esther finally encounters her mother — the scene in the brickmaker's cottage, the recognition scene —
"I looked at her; but I could not see her, I could not hear her, I could not draw my breath."
That is Esther's voice — but it doubles as the reader's own overwhelm.
And Lady Dedlock in that scene is not cold, not bored — she is shattered by what her choices have cost her daughter.
Dickens shows us the bill, and it is a very long one.
Edmund, I love that — 'the bill' — but I want to press on the craft of how that recognition scene is staged.
Because Dickens is doing something technically remarkable with his dual narration throughout the Lady Dedlock plot.
The omniscient narrator shows us Lady Dedlock from the outside — cool, ironic, slightly theatrical.
But we only gain access to her inner life obliquely, through Esther's narration — through the eyes of the daughter she abandoned.
That displacement is not an accident — it is the structural enactment of their estrangement.
We never get Lady Dedlock's interior directly — and that withholding mirrors her own decades-long withholding from the world.
Think of the letter she leaves at the end — her final confession.
"I have no home left. I passed last night in the open air."
Written in her own hand at last — after all the legal documents, the handwriting that betrayed her — she finally speaks in her own voice.
And it is stripped of all ornament.
That letter is also a legal document of a kind — a testimony, addressed to no one, that will be used to condemn her memory even in death.
What Dickens understood — and this is where his legal satire bites deepest — is that for women in this period, there was no neutral space outside the law's reach.
Tulkinghorn doesn't need a courtroom. He only needs knowledge.
And the knowledge he pursues is explicitly about her body, her past, her sexuality — the things the Victorian legal system treated as a woman's defining transgressions.
Dickens captures this when he shows Tulkinghorn's satisfaction not in gold or advancement but simply in the act of knowing what Lady Dedlock cannot prevent him knowing.
He describes Tulkinghorn's rooms as being like himself — full of closed drawers, locked boxes, secrets of every kind.
"Mute, close, irresponsive to any glancing light."
The man is his own filing cabinet — and Lady Dedlock is the most prized document inside it.
That is very good, James — though I note Dickens also gives us Tulkinghorn's death as a kind of divine accounting.
The man who exploited Lady Dedlock's secret is shot in his own rooms, under the painted Roman figure on his ceiling that points its finger at him.
Dickens is not a subtle symbolist — but here the bluntness is entirely appropriate.
What I find most moving about Lady Dedlock — and I insist on moving, not merely pitying — is the final image Dickens gives us of her.
She dies dressed as the brickmaker's wife — as Nemo's lover — stripped of every rank she married into.
She has returned, in her death, to what she truly was.
Dickens gives her that dignity — the dignity of authenticity reclaimed too late.
It is, I think, one of the great tragic endings in the Victorian novel.
Edmund says 'reclaimed too late' — and that timing is everything in this novel's structure.
Dickens stages the discovery of Lady Dedlock's body so that it is Esther and Inspector Bucket who find her — together.
The daughter who has been searching for a mother, and the detective who has been pursuing a fugitive.
Those two quests converge on the same frozen body at the gate of the pauper's graveyard — at the very spot where Captain Hawdon is buried.
She has come back, in death, to the one love she could never safely acknowledge in life.
Esther describes it simply — and it is Dickens at his most devastating when he is at his most plain:
"I passed on to the gate, and stooped down. I lifted the heavy head, put the long dank hair aside, and turned the face. And it was my mother, cold and dead."
Five monosyllables at the end of that sentence — and the whole novel seems to close around them.
Cold and dead — and yet, as the three of you have shown, somehow more fully herself than at any earlier point in the story.
Authenticity arriving, as Edmund says, precisely too late — which may be Dickens' darkest observation about what secrets cost us.
Lady Dedlock stands at the intersection of everything this novel cares about: the law's cruelty, society's hypocrisy, and the private self that survives, barely, beneath the performance.
We'll carry her with us as we move to our next subject — thank you all, and thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

segments.title: Mud, Crossing, and Invisibility: Jo's Voice in Dickensian London

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast where we take Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart sentence by sentence, image by image.
I'm your host, and today we're gathered to discuss one of the most quietly devastating presences in all of English fiction.
Jo — the crossing-sweeper. The boy who don't know nothing.
To help us understand what Dickens is doing with this character — technically, morally, historically — I'm joined by three remarkable minds.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a clock — all the moving parts at once.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows Chancery, the Poor Law, and Victorian London from the inside — the unglamorous inside.
And Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, brings the perspective of a critic who believes Dickens' power is always moral before it is political.
Our subject today: Jo's voice, Jo's world, and what it means to be invisible at the heart of one of the noisiest novels ever written.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — as a writer yourself, what strikes you first about the way Dickens handles Jo on the page?
What strikes me immediately — and it never stops striking me on rereading — is the grammar.
Dickens gives Jo a dialect that is not merely phonetic transcription — it is syntactically broken in a very specific, deliberate way.
Think of the great passage where the narrator describes Jo's state of mind, and Dickens writes in that extraordinary third-person apostrophe.
"It must be a strange state to be like Jo. To shuffle through the streets, unfamiliar with the shapes, and in utter darkness as to the meaning of those mysterious symbols."
Dickens is inhabiting Jo's consciousness from the outside, which is the only honest position he can take — because Jo cannot narrate himself.
And that is the central formal problem the novel is wrestling with — and solving, beautifully, in these passages.
Jo cannot read. Jo cannot write. Jo is, in the most literal sense, outside language.
And yet here he is — in a novel. Speaking. Witnessed. That tension is where the real power lives.
That distinction — witnessed but unable to witness himself — feels crucial to everything that follows.
James, you've spent years in the archives of Victorian social policy. When you meet Jo, what do you see that the novel's first readers would have recognized immediately?
They would have recognized him in an instant — and felt, I suspect, a complicated mixture of guilt and relief at recognizing him.

Crossing-sweepers were everywhere in mid-Victorian London — children who cleared a path through the horse dung and mud so that respectable pedestrians could cross the street without soiling their boots.
Henry Mayhew documented them in extraordinary detail in London Labour and the London Poor, which was appearing at almost exactly the same time Bleak House was being serialized.
The crossing-sweeper occupied a very precise social position — just above absolute destitution, but only just.
What Dickens understood — and this is where he is genuinely sharper than many social reformers of his era — is that this child's invisibility is not accidental.
It is the precondition of his usefulness. You need him not to matter, so that he can keep your boots clean.
And Dickens crystallizes this with terrible precision when the law comes for Jo in chapter eleven — Move on, Jo. Move on.
"I'm always a-moving on, sir. I've always been a-moving and a-moving on ever since I was born."
That is not pathos as decoration. That is an indictment of an entire social system delivered in the voice of a boy who doesn't know he's making one.
I would not wish to quarrel with the historical context — Blackstone has set it out admirably — but I think we risk losing something essential if we read Jo purely as a social document.
Dickens' genius with Jo is not primarily forensic. It is — if I may use the word without embarrassment — spiritual.
Consider the passage where Jo is asked by the inquest whether he knows what an oath is, what a prayer is, what the Almighty is.
"It's a swearing to tell the truth." "Have you any idea of the nature of an oath?" And the coroner dismisses him — because Jo knows nothing of the form.
What Dickens is drawing here is not merely legal exclusion — it is a portrait of moral innocence that the society around Jo has systematically failed to educate into knowledge.
Jo is not ignorant because the system is cruel. Jo is ignorant because no individual human being has ever thought him worth the effort of teaching.
That is a distinction with a very real moral weight, and Dickens — to his immense credit — does not let either explanation off the hook.
Edmund's point about spiritual innocence is exactly right, and I think the craft choice that enforces it is the narrator's direct address to the reader.
Dickens breaks the fictional frame entirely in those Jo chapters — he wheels on the reader as both judge and accused.
He sets it up like an indictment — listen to how the prose shifts into a kind of legal liturgy.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order."
The anaphora — Dead, Dead, Dead — is both a funeral bell and a legal charge sheet. It is rhetorical genius.
And notice how Dickens corrupts the honorifics — Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends — in the same breath.
He is making the Church itself stand accused alongside the law, alongside the comfortable classes. No one is exempt from that sentence.
And yet — forgive me, Eleanor — that passage is sometimes read as mere rhetoric, as if the anger were its own justification.
What makes it historically and humanly devastating is the specific detail that precedes it — smallpox.
Jo contracts smallpox at Tom-all-Alone's — that rookery, that festering pocket of London which Dickens constructs as a kind of anti-Chancery, a chaos without even the pretense of system.
He then passes the infection to Esther Summerson — the novel's moral center — who is permanently disfigured.
That is not symbol. That is epidemiology. Dickens had read the public health reports — he knew that disease did not respect class boundaries.
Tom-all-Alone's taking its revenge on those who ignored it — that is the phrase Dickens uses, almost exactly, and it rings like a prophecy.
"There is not a drop of Tom's corrupted blood but propagates infection and contagion somewhere."
The slum takes its revenge. Not metaphorically. Literally, biologically, on the bodies of the comfortable.
Blackstone is right about the epidemiology, and I would not understate it. But I will insist on something the social reading can overlook.
Jo's death — and it is one of the great deaths in English fiction — is not primarily a political event. It is a sacramental one.
Allan Woodcourt sits with Jo at the end — a doctor, a man of genuine goodness — and he tries to teach the boy the Lord's Prayer.
"Our Father. Say it after me." And Jo, dying, tries to repeat it — gets partway through — and is gone.
That moment is not an argument about the Poor Law. It is a question put to the universe about whether grace can reach those whom society has placed entirely beyond its reach.
And Dickens — who was not, I think, a conventionally pious man — gives us no comfortable answer.
Jo dies learning to pray. Whether his prayer arrives anywhere is left — as all the most honest art leaves such things — in silence.
That silence is actually engineered in the prose, and it's worth dwelling on the sentence that falls immediately after Jo's death.
Dickens writes — and this is one of the most discussed sentences in Victorian literature — the narrator's direct intrusion.
"Dead, Jo. Dead, Jo. Dead!"
Three words, repeated. The narrator drops every pretense of fictional distance and speaks to the boy directly.
For the first and only time, the narrator acknowledges Jo not as subject, not as case study, but as — you.
It's a posthumous recognition. The novel sees Jo clearly at the moment when seeing him can no longer help him at all.
A posthumous recognition. That phrase will stay with me.
James, Edmund, Eleanor — you've given us Jo as social fact, as moral test, and as a formal problem that the novel solves and refuses to solve at the same time.
What I hear in all three of your readings is that Jo's power comes precisely from his position at the edge of the novel's language — not quite speakable, not quite silent.

In our next segment, we'll follow that fog outward — from Tom-all-Alone's into Chancery itself — and ask what the great case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce is actually doing to the living people trapped inside it.

segments.title: The Machinery of Ruin: Richard's Choices and Moral Decline

utterances.text: Now we turn to one of the novel's great tragic arcs — Richard Carstone.
A young man of real charm and genuine ability who is slowly consumed by a lawsuit he did not choose and a hope he cannot relinquish.
Eleanor, you've written about the way Dickens constructs decline — what draws you to Richard as a study in that?
Richard is one of the most carefully engineered characters in the whole of Dickens — which is saying something.
The tragedy isn't sudden. It's constructed in small increments, each chapter slightly worse than the last.
Dickens gives Richard every advantage at the outset — looks, warmth, intelligence — and then watches Chancery take them one by one.
There's a line Esther gives us early on, in her narration, about Richard's restlessness — that he possessed a certain quality of being 'always beginning.'
'He had not that quality which we may call, for want of a better name, solidity.'
That word — solidity — is doing so much work. It's not a moral failing yet. It's a constitutional vulnerability.
Dickens locates the flaw before the lawsuit ever gets its hooks in, and that's what makes the decline feel inevitable rather than imposed.
I'd push on that word 'inevitable' just slightly, because I think it lets Chancery off the hook.
Richard's constitutional restlessness is real — Eleanor's right about that — but Jarndyce and Jarndyce is the machinery that converts a personal weakness into absolute ruin.
The suit offers him something extraordinarily dangerous: a reason to defer all effort, all commitment, all responsibility to an imagined future settlement.
Dickens understood exactly how the Court of Chancery worked — or rather, didn't work — and that understanding sharpens every scene Richard appears in.
Cases in equity could run for generations without resolution. Richard's hope is not irrational — it's historically plausible.
And that historical plausibility is what makes Dickens's satire so lethal.
The system doesn't need to lie to Richard. It only needs to go on existing exactly as it does.
I appreciate James's institutional analysis, but I must resist the implication that Richard is primarily a victim of the system.
Jarndyce himself — a man formed by the very same suit — demonstrates that Chancery need not be determinative of character.
The novel presents us with a clear moral contrast: Jarndyce turns away from the suit and achieves something approaching wisdom; Richard turns toward it and is destroyed.
Dickens is too honest a moralist to suggest there is no element of will involved.
Consider the scene where Jarndyce warns Richard directly — and Richard receives the counsel with apparent gratitude and then proceeds to ignore it entirely.
Jarndyce says, in effect, 'Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts.'
Richard hears it. He simply cannot act upon it. And that, to my mind, is the tragedy — a failure of moral will, not merely social circumstance.
I think Edmund and James are both right, and that's precisely where Dickens is at his most sophisticated.
He refuses to resolve the tension between system and self. The novel holds both accountable simultaneously.
What I find structurally brilliant is the way Dickens uses the career-switching — law, medicine, the army — to dramatise Richard's evasion.
Each new profession is a fresh beginning that isn't really a beginning at all — it's a postponement in disguise.
And Esther sees it. She renders it with such painful precision — watching someone she loves recede from himself.
There's that devastating moment when she observes that his handsome face had grown thin, and his manner restless and hurried.
'He had the brightest and most handsome face I ever saw... but it had an anxious, haggard expression.'
That physical deterioration is the outer narrative of an inner collapse. The body becomes a kind of ledger for moral debt.
The ledger metaphor is apt, because money is very much the material reality behind Richard's collapse.
He borrows against his expectations — which is to say, against nothing. Vholes encourages this. Sustains it.
Vholes is one of Dickens's great portraits of institutional predation dressed up as professional service.
His manner of speaking to Richard is always measured, always sombre — always feeding the delusion while billing by the hour.
Dickens gives Vholes a marvellous line — something to the effect that he has a father in the Vale of Taunton and three daughters to support.
'I am not a self-interested man. I have a father in the Vale of Taunton. I have three daughters.'
He invokes his own dependants as a moral alibi for stripping Richard of everything. The audacity of it is magnificent — and appalling.
The real obscenity is that Vholes is perfectly legal. Perfectly respectable. And the system protects him absolutely.
I find Vholes entirely convincing as a satirical portrait, and I shan't defend him.
But I would observe that Richard chooses Vholes. He seeks him out. He dismisses Jarndyce's solicitors — who were honest men — in favour of someone who will tell him what he wishes to hear.
That choice is a moral event of the first order, and the novel treats it as such.
What strikes me as the most moving moment in Richard's entire story is his death scene — the way he achieves a kind of clarity only when all hope has been extinguished.
When the suit finally collapses — consuming itself and all its costs — Richard says to Jarndyce with extraordinary simplicity:
'I will begin the world.'
Five words. All those wasted years, all that accumulated ruin — and at last, he is ready to begin.
Except that he cannot. He dies within hours. And that irony is not satirical — it is genuinely tragic.
'I will begin the world.' Edmund, that's the line that breaks me every time.
Because it echoes every earlier false start. Every new profession, every new scheme. He has been 'beginning' his entire adult life.
And now, for the first and only time, he means it without qualification — and it's too late.
The dual narration makes this even richer. Esther can't witness his death directly — it happens offstage, relayed through others.
Which is formally perfect, because Esther's whole relationship to Richard has been one of watching from a slight distance, unable to intervene.
The structure of the narration enacts the tragedy. That's Dickens at his absolute best.
And Ada — Richard's wife, watching all of this — is herself a kind of silent tragedy within the tragedy.
James, the women in Richard's orbit — Ada, Esther — do they function differently as witnesses to his decline?
Ada is in a genuinely impossible position — one that the law of coverture makes concrete.
Once she marries Richard secretly, her legal identity merges with his. His ruin is her ruin, by statute.
She spends her own money — the little she has — trying to sustain him, and the novel treats this with great tenderness but no illusions.
The secret marriage is in some ways the cruelest plot turn — not because Richard is wicked, but because it removes the last external check on his behaviour.
Jarndyce could counsel him. Ada can only love him. And love, in this novel, is not enough to save a man from himself.
The secret marriage is the moment where Richard's evasion becomes something more actively harmful than mere self-destruction.
He draws Ada into his ruin without giving her the chance to choose otherwise — and that is a moral failure of a different order.
And yet — and this is what makes Dickens a great novelist rather than a moralist — he never makes Richard entirely unsympathetic.
There is genuine warmth between Richard and Esther throughout. His affection for Ada is real. His charm never quite deserts him.
Dickens understood — as Burke understood about the nature of political virtue — that character is not a simple sum of good and bad qualities.
It is a configuration. And what Chancery destroys in Richard is the configuration — not the individual qualities, but the balance between them.
A configuration destroyed by patience — or rather by a system that makes patience impossible.
Richard Carstone stands as one of Dickens's most fully realised studies in the catastrophe of deferred living.
And as our three guests have shown today, his story refuses to be reduced to either individual failing or systemic cruelty — it insists on being both.
Coming up next, we'll turn to Esther Summerson herself — narrator, participant, and the moral centre that holds this sprawling novel together.

segments.title: Networks of Revelation: How Dickens Weaves Plot and Character

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great sprawling masterwork apart — carefully — to see how it actually works.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a question that sits at the very heart of the novel: how does Dickens make a plot of such extraordinary complexity feel not only coherent, but inevitable?
The theme is Networks of Revelation — the way secrets, connections, and characters weave together across sixty-seven chapters until everything, at last, is disclosed.
To explore this, I have three brilliant guides with me.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and has a gift — rare among critics — for making the architecture of a novel feel as thrilling as its story.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows Victorian institutions from the inside out — and who will remind us, I suspect, that the Jarndyce suit was not Dickens' invention so much as his diagnosis.
And Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, Tory of the old school, and the most careful close reader in the room — who believes Bleak House is ultimately a novel about character, not system.
Let's begin with the most basic question — and therefore the hardest: how does Dickens hold this together at all?
It's a fair question, and I think the honest answer is that Dickens holds it together the way a spider holds a web — through tension rather than rigidity.
The structural genius of Bleak House is that every character is also a secret — and every secret has at least two characters whose lives it will detonate when it surfaces.

Think about Lady Dedlock alone — she is simultaneously the revelation that will destroy her, the mystery that drives Tulkinghorn, the truth that will remake Esther's identity, and the ghost that haunts the whole Dedlock estate.
Dickens constructs her as a node — if you'll forgive the term — in about four different narrative networks at once.
And the early chapters are brilliantly patient about this — they give us her stillness, her magnificent boredom, before we have any idea what she's concealing.
There's that wonderful moment in chapter two — Dickens tells us she has found her country seat, Chesney Wold, 'quite dull.'
'My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in familiar conversation, her place in Lincolnshire.'
That phrase — 'what she calls, in familiar conversation, her place' — is loaded with irony before we even understand what it costs her to own it.
Eleanor is right that the secret is the structural unit — but I'd push it further and say it's specifically the legal secret, the document, the will, the written record.
Bleak House is, at its structural core, a novel about paper — about what happens when a society produces so many documents that no one can any longer say which ones are real.
Chancery runs on paper — pleadings, affidavits, schedules of costs — and the Jarndyce suit is not simply a legal case; it is a document that eats people alive.
The detective plot — Tulkinghorn's investigation, Bucket's investigation — is, at every turn, a search for a particular piece of paper.
Lady Dedlock is undone by a handwriting sample — a scrap of legal correspondence her lover Hawdon wrote before he became Nemo, the nobody who copied documents in a slum.
Dickens saw this clearly — that in Victorian England, your fate could be sealed by what was or was not written about you.
He has that savage description of Krook's shop, where the walls are thick with mouldering papers — legal waste, but waste that might contain everything.
'He is rarely out of his shop. It is his house, his home, his all.'
Krook himself is of course the Lord Chancellor in miniature — presiding over documents he cannot read, which is Dickens' most economical satirical stroke in the entire book.
James makes a compelling case for paper as mechanism — and it is perfectly true that documents drive the plot machinery.
But I would suggest that what actually holds the novel together is something altogether more classical — it is character destiny.
In the great novelistic tradition from Fielding through Austen, the plot is a machine for revealing what characters were always going to be.
Richard Carstone is not destroyed by the Chancery suit — he is destroyed by a weakness of will that Chancery merely provides occasion to exercise.
Dickens signals this with enormous care from Richard's very first appearance — that charming, changeable, finally tragic incapacity for settled purpose.
And John Jarndyce is the novel's moral centre precisely because he has chosen — actively chosen — not to be consumed by the thing that would consume Richard.
Dickens writes of him, in one of the finest formulations in the book, that he regards the suit as something one ought simply to endure — and endurance, in Dickens, is a form of heroism.
'Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good that has ever come of it.'
That line says everything about Jarndyce's moral intelligence — he has made peace with absurdity by transforming it into dark comedy.

Edmund, I find I agree with you about Richard more than I expected to — but I want to press on the dual narrative, because I think that's where the revelatory network becomes most technically audacious.
You have two narrative voices: the third-person omniscient narrator, present tense, ironic, almost cinematically sweeping — and then Esther, first person, past tense, modest, provisional.
What's extraordinary is that Esther narrates her own story without knowing the largest facts about it — she doesn't know her mother's identity for a very long time.
So the reader holds a double consciousness throughout — we know things about Esther's world that Esther herself cannot yet see.

The third-person narrator has already shown us Lady Dedlock startled by the handwriting before Esther ever meets her — so when Esther finally describes Lady Dedlock's face, we feel the revelation before she does.
Esther says, with her characteristic understatement, that she could not account for a 'strange' feeling when she looked at her — that is Dickens constructing irony through narrative innocence.
'I had a curious sensation of having seen her before.'
Five words — 'having seen her before' — and they carry the weight of an entire secret history that is about to reshape the novel.
That doubleness Eleanor describes has, I think, a specific social dimension that's easy to miss if you read the novel purely as a formal experiment.
Esther's ignorance of her own origins is not merely a narrative device — it is the exact condition of hundreds of thousands of illegitimate children in mid-Victorian England.
They existed without legal identity — no birth certificate, no acknowledged parentage, no inheritance rights — they were, in the legal sense, nobody's children.
And the word Dickens uses for Hawdon — Nemo — Latin for nobody — is not accidental.
Esther's father is a legal non-entity, and her mother's secret is kept precisely by the machinery of class and law that Chancery represents.
The network of revelation Dickens builds is, in this sense, also a map of what Victorian society was organized to conceal.
Jo the crossing-sweeper is perhaps the most devastating example — he knows Hawdon's grave, he is a living link in the chain, but he cannot read, cannot testify, cannot count in the eyes of the law.
Dickens gives him one of the most heartbreaking lines in all of Victorian fiction — the coroner dismisses him from the inquest into Hawdon's death.
'Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don't know that everybody has two names.'
A child who doesn't know he is supposed to have a surname — that is Dickens' indictment of the entire social order in a single sentence.
James moves me — I confess it — and Jo's death is one of the passages in English literature that I find genuinely difficult to read without emotion.
But I would resist the reduction of that passage to a sociological exhibit — the power of Jo's death comes from what Dickens does with it morally and spiritually.
Jo dies trying to repeat a prayer he has barely grasped — taught to him by Woodcourt — and Dickens transforms that stumbling recitation into something genuinely sacred.
The authorial voice then rises in one of those extraordinary direct addresses to the reader that Dickens permits himself only at the highest pitch of feeling.
'Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order.'
'Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day.'
That is not sociology — that is lamentation, the form the Hebrew prophets used when human institutions had failed so completely that only direct address to the conscience would do.
Edmund has just made me love that passage even more, which I didn't think was possible.
But I want to pick up the thread about the plot network — because I think Inspector Bucket is the moment when Dickens makes the network itself the subject.
Bucket is the first great detective in English fiction — and what defines him is that he can see the whole network at once.
He moves through every class, every household, every secret — he is the only character who occupies every strand of the web simultaneously.
His famous pointing forefinger — Dickens keeps returning to it — is the image of a mind that connects, that gestures toward the thing others cannot yet see.
Dickens introduces him almost subliminally in an earlier chapter before he steps forward — he's present at the Dedlock dinner before we know who he is.
That is deliberate structural preparation — Bucket is already watching the network before the network knows it needs to be watched.
Bucket is a fascinating figure from a historical standpoint — the Metropolitan Police was only founded in 1829, and the Detective Branch in 1842, just a decade before Bleak House.
Dickens was personally fascinated by the new detective police — he wrote admiringly about Inspector Field, who was almost certainly the model for Bucket.
What made Bucket radical — in the social sense — was precisely what Eleanor identifies: he crosses class lines with impunity, and no one can quite refuse him.
He arrests Sir Leicester Dedlock's intimate associate Tulkinghorn's murderer — Mr. George, a soldier, a man of ostensible respectability — in the same week he hunts a fugitive through the slums.
And crucially, his power comes from information — from the accumulated knowledge of who is connected to whom.

Dickens writes him as surprisingly sympathetic when he arrests George — firm, even gentle — and that is a carefully calibrated moral signal about legitimate versus illegitimate uses of institutional power.
I would add that Bucket's limitation is also his profoundest interest as a character — he can solve the murder, but he cannot save Lady Dedlock.
He and Esther hunt her through the winter night — that extraordinary chapter, one of the finest pieces of sustained narrative tension Dickens ever wrote — and they arrive too late.
And Lady Dedlock is found dead at the gate of the paupers' burial ground where Hawdon lies — she has, in death, insisted on her connection to the man and the life she was forced to renounce.
The detective cannot penetrate the inner life — that is always beyond him — and the revelation of the network ultimately comes too late for the person it most concerns.
Dickens writes it with devastating restraint — Esther recognizes her mother only after death, only after it is irreversibly too late.
'I passed on to the gate, and stooped down. I lifted the heavy head, put the long dank hair aside, and turned the face. And it was my mother, cold and dead.'
Three short declarative sentences — 'cold and dead' — after six hundred pages of concealment. The revelation, when it comes, is silence.
That is a remarkable place to pause — and I think it captures something essential about what we've been circling all conversation.
The network of revelation in Bleak House doesn't deliver triumph — it delivers truth, and truth arrives, often as not, in the form of a loss.

We've heard from Eleanor about the structural audacity of the dual narrative, from James about the social and legal conditions that make secrets possible, and from Edmund about the moral and spiritual weight that Dickens insists secrets carry.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the fog itself — that great opening image — and ask what Dickens is doing when he makes a city's atmosphere the first character his readers encounter.

segments.title: Bleak House's Bitter Irony: System, Suffering, and the Novel's Vision

utterances.text: We've spent today deep inside the fog — Chancery's fog, London's fog, the fog of self-deception and systemic cruelty.
Before we close, I want to ask each of you what you think Dickens ultimately wants us to feel — and do — at the end of this extraordinary novel.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because I think the question of what Bleak House finally asks of its reader is, at heart, a formal question as much as a moral one.
That's exactly right, and it's what makes the novel so unsettling even after you close the last page.
Dickens gives us two endings, structurally speaking — Esther's quiet happiness at the new Bleak House, and the third-person narrator's cold, annihilating summation of Chancery's devastation.
Those two tones refuse to resolve into each other — and I think that irresolution is deliberate architecture.
Consider how the novel closes the Jarndyce case — not with triumph, but with the estate entirely consumed by legal costs.
"The costs have swallowed up the whole estate — the suit lapses and melts away."
Melts away — that verb is doing everything.
All those decades of hope and ruin simply dissolve, like the fog itself, as though they never were.
That's not satire — that's elegy.
Eleanor is right that it's elegy — but I'd insist it's also indictment, and the two are entirely compatible.
What strikes me, returning to the novel, is how precisely calibrated the suffering is to the actual mechanics of Chancery practice.
The delays, the bills of costs, the interminable discovery — Dickens knew the machinery from the inside, and he rendered it without exaggeration.
And then there is Jo — the crossing-sweeper — who I think is the moral centre the novel keeps returning to.
Dickens steps entirely outside the Jarndyce plot to apostrophise him — to speak to us directly about what this child's death means.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order."
That repeated 'Dead' is a drumbeat — aimed at every institution and rank that failed him.
And then the line that follows — 'and dying thus around us every day' — makes Jo not a single case but a condition.
That is the bitter irony at the novel's core: the system that cannot see Jo is the same system administering justice to the parties in Jarndyce.
I won't quarrel with the power of that passage — it is among the most devastating in the English novel.
But I should enter a gentle caveat against reading Bleak House purely as a brief for institutional reform.
Dickens was, I think, far more interested in what suffering reveals about individual souls than in drafting a programme for Parliament.
Consider Esther Summerson — the character most critics either take for granted or condescend to — who is, in fact, the novel's supreme moral achievement.
She cannot reform Chancery, she cannot save Richard — but she can act well, in full knowledge that circumstance may defeat her.
Dickens gives her that extraordinary moment of self-examination after her illness, where she describes herself looking in the glass.
"I had never been a beauty and had never thought myself one; but I had been very different from this."
The quietness of that acceptance is almost unbearable — and it has nothing to do with Chancery.
It has to do with what Johnson called the dignity of endurance — the moral life lived under conditions not of one's choosing.
That, for me, is where the novel's bitterest and most sustaining irony lies: in the gap between what the system is and what a single good person can still become within it.
Edmund, I find that genuinely moving — and I think you've touched something real about Esther.
But I'd push back slightly: the novel's form itself insists on the system.
Every time we're in Esther's first-person warmth, Dickens cuts to the omniscient narrator's savage third-person irony — and the cutting is the argument.
He doesn't let us rest inside Esther's goodness.
He keeps dragging us back to Krook's spontaneous combustion, to Tom-all-Alone's, to the Dedlock scandal — to everything that Esther's quiet virtue cannot touch.
The very opening of the book sets the terms — 'London. Michaelmas Term lately over' — that flat judicial announcement before the fog descends.
"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth."
That's Genesis inverted — creation undone, primordial chaos restored — all before we've met a single character.
Esther's private goodness is real and necessary — but it exists inside that.
And that, I think, is where the bitter irony sharpens into something almost unbearable for a historically-minded reader.
Chancery was reformed — the Judicature Acts of the 1870s effectively abolished the system Dickens described.
But Tom-all-Alone's was not reformed — the urban poverty Dickens anatomised persisted for generations.
Dickens knows this, I think — which is why the irony runs deeper than institutional satire.
The link he draws between the ruinous slum and Chancery — 'Jo has not yet died' — is a statement about the interconnection of neglect.
"There is not an atom of Tom's slum — not a cubic inch of any pestilential gas — which shall work its retribution."
Retribution — not reform.
The system doesn't just fail the poor — it poisons everyone downstream, including the Dedlocks, including Richard, including ultimately Sir Leicester in his desolate paralysis.
Sir Leicester — there, I confess, Dickens achieves something extraordinary that no polemicist could manage.
He gives us a man who is in many respects absurd — pompous, fossilised, utterly wrong about almost everything political — and then devastates us with his love for Lady Dedlock.
When he learns of her disgrace — and forgives her entirely, without condition — Dickens has him speak with a tenderness one would not have thought him capable of.
"She is my wife, loved and honoured. I require no other knowledge."
Six words.
Six words that demolish everything we thought we knew about this man — and that is entirely outside the system's remit.
That is the moral imagination James was too busy drafting reform legislation to credit.
No act of Parliament produces that moment — only a novelist of genius does.
I shall accept that rebuke with characteristic dignity.
And Edmund is right — the Leicester scene is the novel's great surprise, its most generous irony.
But perhaps that's exactly the layered argument Dickens is making — that individuals can transcend their systems in moments of grace, while the systems themselves grind on regardless.
Which is, when you think about it, precisely why the ending doesn't comfort us.
Esther gets her happiness — her dear name, her new Bleak House, Woodcourt's love — and it's real, it's earned, and we feel it.
But the omniscient narrator's final note on Chancery — that suite of devastations — runs underneath it like a ground bass.
Dickens refuses the consolation of the happy ending as sufficient answer to the world's cruelty.
That dual-narrator structure isn't just technique — it's the novel's moral position, built into the form.
And on that note — a moral position built into form itself — I think we've arrived at the heart of what makes Bleak House endure.
A novel that contains within it both Esther's quiet joy and Jo's annihilating death — and refuses to let either cancel the other out.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Edmund Leigh — three readers who've brought intelligence, passion, and genuine disagreement to every page of this remarkable novel.
Bleak House Unpacked has been a production of the Literary Archive series.
If the fog has lifted a little — or thickened wonderfully — do join us for our next episode.
Until then — thank you for listening.

Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in
course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it
means. The parties to it understand it least, but it has been
observed that no two Chancery lawyers can talk about it for five
minutes without coming to a total disagreement as to all the
premises. Innumerable children have been born into the cause;
innumerable young people have married into it; innumerable old people
have died out of it. Scores of persons have deliriously found
themselves made parties in Jarndyce and Jarndyce without knowing how
or why; whole families have inherited legendary hatreds with the
suit. The little plaintiff or defendant who was promised a new
rocking-horse when Jarndyce and Jarndyce should be settled has grown
up, possessed himself of a real horse, and trotted away into the
other world. Fair wards of court have faded into mothers and
grandmothers; a long procession of Chancellors has come in and gone
out; the legion of bills in the suit have been transformed into mere
bills of mortality; there are not three Jarndyces left upon the earth
perhaps since old Tom Jarndyce in despair blew his brains out at a

interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”

My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days
previous to her departure for Paris, where her ladyship intends to
stay some weeks, after which her movements are uncertain. The
fashionable intelligence says so for the comfort of the Parisians,
and it knows all fashionable things. To know things otherwise were to
be unfashionable. My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in
familiar conversation, her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are
out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been
sapped and sopped away. The adjacent low-lying ground for half a mile
in breadth is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands in
it and a surface punctured all over, all day long, with falling rain.
My Lady Dedlock’s place has been extremely dreary. The weather for
many a day and night has been so wet that the trees seem wet through,
and the soft loppings and prunings of the woodman’s axe can make no
crash or crackle as they fall. The deer, looking soaked, leave
quagmires where they pass. The shot of a rifle loses its sharpness in
the moist air, and its smoke moves in a tardy little cloud towards
the green rise, coppice-topped, that makes a background for the
falling rain. The view from my Lady Dedlock’s own windows is
alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink. The vases
on the stone terrace in the foreground catch the rain all day; and
the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the broad flagged
pavement, called from old time the Ghost’s Walk, all night. On
Sundays the little church in the park is mouldy; the oaken pulpit
breaks out into a cold sweat; and there is a general smell and taste
as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady Dedlock (who is
childless), looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a
keeper’s lodge and seeing the light of a fire upon the latticed
panes, and smoke rising from the chimney, and a child, chased by a
woman, running out into the rain to meet the shining figure of a
wrapped-up man coming through the gate, has been put quite out of
temper. My Lady Dedlock says she has been “bored to death.”

It must be a strange state to be like Jo! To shuffle through the
streets, unfamiliar with the shapes, and in utter darkness as to the
meaning, of those mysterious symbols, so abundant over the shops, and
at the corners of streets, and on the doors, and in the windows! To
see people read, and to see people write, and to see the postmen
deliver letters, and not to have the least idea of all that
language—to be, to every scrap of it, stone blind and dumb! It must
be very puzzling to see the good company going to the churches on
Sundays, with their books in their hands, and to think (for perhaps
Jo DOES think at odd times) what does it all mean, and if it means
anything to anybody, how comes it that it means nothing to me? To be
hustled, and jostled, and moved on; and really to feel that it would
appear to be perfectly true that I have no business here, or there,
or anywhere; and yet to be perplexed by the consideration that I AM
here somehow, too, and everybody overlooked me until I became the
creature that I am! It must be a strange state, not merely to be told
that I am scarcely human (as in the case of my offering myself for a
witness), but to feel it of my own knowledge all my life! To see the
horses, dogs, and cattle go by me and to know that in ignorance I
belong to them and not to the superior beings in my shape, whose
delicacy I offend! Jo’s ideas of a criminal trial, or a judge, or a
bishop, or a government, or that inestimable jewel to him (if he only
knew it) the Constitution, should be strange! His whole material and
immaterial life is wonderfully strange; his death, the strangest
thing of all.
c16:p11.summary: The narrator powerfully explores Jo's alienation from literate society, meaning-making, and human dignity, showing how systemic exclusion has made him feel less than human.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,

my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for

“Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet,” proceeds Mr. Bucket, who delights
in a full title and does violence to himself when he dispenses with
any fragment of it, “the last point in the case which I am now going
to mention shows the necessity of patience in our business, and never
doing a thing in a hurry. I watched this young woman yesterday
without her knowledge when she was looking at the funeral, in company
with my wife, who planned to take her there; and I had so much to
convict her, and I saw such an expression in her face, and my mind so
rose against her malice towards her ladyship, and the time was
altogether such a time for bringing down what you may call
retribution upon her, that if I had been a younger hand with less
experience, I should have taken her, certain. Equally, last night,
when her ladyship, as is so universally admired I am sure, come home
looking—why, Lord, a man might almost say like Venus rising from the
ocean—it was so unpleasant and inconsistent to think of her being
charged with a murder of which she was innocent that I felt quite to
want to put an end to the job. What should I have lost? Sir Leicester
Dedlock, Baronet, I should have lost the weapon. My prisoner here
proposed to Mrs. Bucket, after the departure of the funeral, that
they should go per bus a little ways into the country and take tea at
a very decent house of entertainment. Now, near that house of
entertainment there’s a piece of water. At tea, my prisoner got up to
fetch her pocket-handkercher from the bedroom where the bonnets was;
she was rather a long time gone and came back a little out of wind.
As soon as they came home this was reported to me by Mrs. Bucket,
along with her observations and suspicions. I had the piece of water
dragged by moonlight, in presence of a couple of our men, and the
pocket pistol was brought up before it had been there half-a-dozen
hours. Now, my dear, put your arm a little further through mine, and
hold it steady, and I shan’t hurt you!”

and there are two or three maces, or petty-bags, or privy purses, or
whatever they may be, in legal court suits. These are all yawning,
for no crumb of amusement ever falls from Jarndyce and Jarndyce (the
cause in hand), which was squeezed dry years upon years ago. The
short-hand writers, the reporters of the court, and the reporters of
the newspapers invariably decamp with the rest of the regulars when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce comes on. Their places are a blank. Standing on
a seat at the side of the hall, the better to peer into the curtained
sanctuary, is a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet who is
always in court, from its sitting to its rising, and always expecting
some incomprehensible judgment to be given in her favour. Some say
she really is, or was, a party to a suit, but no one knows for
certain because no one cares. She carries some small litter in a
reticule which she calls her documents, principally consisting of
paper matches and dry lavender. A sallow prisoner has come up, in
custody, for the half-dozenth time to make a personal application “to
purge himself of his contempt,” which, being a solitary surviving
executor who has fallen into a state of conglomeration about accounts
of which it is not pretended that he had ever any knowledge, he is
not at all likely ever to do. In the meantime his prospects in life
are ended. Another ruined suitor, who periodically appears from
Shropshire and breaks out into efforts to address the Chancellor at
the close of the day’s business and who can by no means be made to
understand that the Chancellor is legally ignorant of his existence
after making it desolate for a quarter of a century, plants himself
in a good place and keeps an eye on the judge, ready to call out “My
Lord!” in a voice of sonorous complaint on the instant of his rising.
A few lawyers’ clerks and others who know this suitor by sight linger
on the chance of his furnishing some fun and enlivening the dismal
weather a little.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

While Ada was speaking to him in reply, I glanced (I need not say
with how much interest) at his face. It was a handsome, lively, quick
face, full of change and motion; and his hair was a silvered
iron-grey. I took him to be nearer sixty than fifty, but he was
upright, hearty, and robust. From the moment of his first speaking to
us his voice had connected itself with an association in my mind that
I could not define; but now, all at once, a something sudden in his
manner and a pleasant expression in his eyes recalled the gentleman
in the stagecoach six years ago on the memorable day of my journey to
Reading. I was certain it was he. I never was so frightened in my
life as when I made the discovery, for he caught my glance, and
appearing to read my thoughts, gave such a look at the door that I
thought we had lost him.

coming to, that we are plunging down precipices, that now here is

c10:p10.text:
Here, beneath the painted ceiling, with foreshortened Allegory
staring down at his intrusion as if it meant to swoop upon him, and
he cutting it dead, Mr. Tulkinghorn has at once his house and office.
He keeps no staff, only one middle-aged man, usually a little out at
elbows, who sits in a high pew in the hall and is rarely overburdened
with business. Mr. Tulkinghorn is not in a common way. He wants no
clerks. He is a great reservoir of confidences, not to be so tapped.
His clients want HIM; he is all in all. Drafts that he requires to be
drawn are drawn by special-pleaders in the temple on mysterious
instructions; fair copies that he requires to be made are made at the
stationers’, expense being no consideration. The middle-aged man in
the pew knows scarcely more of the affairs of the peerage than any
crossing-sweeper in Holborn.

c1:p8.text:
Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good
that has ever come of it. It has been death to many, but it is a joke
in the profession. Every master in Chancery has had a reference out
of it. Every Chancellor was “in it,” for somebody or other, when he
was counsel at the bar. Good things have been said about it by
blue-nosed, bulbous-shoed old benchers in select port-wine committee
after dinner in hall. Articled clerks have been in the habit of
fleshing their legal wit upon it. The last Lord Chancellor handled it
neatly, when, correcting Mr. Blowers, the eminent silk gown who said
that such a thing might happen when the sky rained potatoes, he
observed, “or when we get through Jarndyce and Jarndyce, Mr.
Blowers”—a pleasantry that particularly tickled the maces, bags, and
purses.
c1:p8.summary: The legal profession treats Jarndyce and Jarndyce as an endless source of witty commentary and profit; even the Lord Chancellor has made pleasantries about it, including a quip that 'tickled the maces, bags, and purses.'
